content: Thioamides, also occasionally referred to as thionamides, are a class of organic compounds characterized by a shared functional group with the general structure R1-CS-NR2R3. One of the most effective methods for synthesizing thioamides involves the reaction of an amide with Lawesson's reagent. Thioamides are also utilized as a class of pharmacological agents to manage thyrotoxicosis. In addition, thioamides can be incorporated into peptides as isosteric replacements for the amide bond. Such peptide modifications serve as intriguing analogues of native peptides, which can provide valuable insights into the structure-activity relationship (SAR). Furthermore, peptide analogues containing thioamides may be developed as drugs with enhanced oral bioavailability. Mechanism of Action Thioamides exert their pharmacological effects by inhibiting the enzyme thyroid peroxidase within the thyroid gland. This inhibition reduces the synthesis of the thyroid hormones triiodothyronine (T3) and thyroxine (T4). Additionally, thioamides block the uptake of iodotyrosines from the colloid and prevent the release of iodine from peripheral thyroid hormone stores. The maximum therapeutic effects of thioamides are observed only after approximately one month of treatment, as the depletion of thyroid hormones occurs gradually due to the reduced synthesis, which is inherently a slow process. Adverse Effects Thioamides are capable of crossing the placental barrier, necessitating caution when administered during pregnancy. Approximately 10% of patients report dermatological side effects, such as skin eruptions presenting as macules and papules. A rare but serious adverse effect, agranulocytosis, occurs in approximately 0.3% of all patients treated with thioamides. This condition is potentially life-threatening and requires immediate medical attention.
